newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. chief promises to take action on Rwanda court.
newsitem.headline: U.N. chief promises to take action on Rwanda court.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan said on Thursday he would discipline U.N. officials if necessary in response to a scathing report of mismanagement and other abuses in the U.N. tribunal on genocide in Rwanda.
"If disciplinary action is required, we will take disciplinary action," he told a news conference. "We are going to move expeditiously and if need be it would include disciplinary actions."

Wednesday's report by Karl Paschke, a German diplomat who heads the U.N. Office of Internal Oversight Services, said the court was riddled with mismanagement, waste, unqualified personnel and bureaucratic infighting.
"Not a single administrative area functioned effectively," he said.

Created by the U.N. Security Council more than two years ago, the tribunal is to try leaders responsible for more than half a million Tutsis and moderate Hutus massacred in Rwanda in 1994 by Hutu troops and others.
The court has indicted 21 people and is currently conducting its first trial in Arusha, Tanzania. A sub-office for prosecutors and investigators is in Kigali, Rwanda.
The United Nations has frequently been accused of tolerating bureaucratic imcompetence and the controversy over the tribunal is bound to develop into a test case for Annan.
He has called three senior officials to New York on Feb. 21, including Prosecutor Louise Arbor of Canada, Deputy Prosecutor Honoure Rakotomanana of Madagascar and Registrar Andronico Adede of Kenya.
Arbor is also chief prosecutor for the U.N. tribunal on war crimes in the former Yugoslavia and is based in The Hague.

U.N. sources said she would probably not renew the contract of Rakotomanana when it expired in March. Paschke in the report criticised his Kigali office for bad management and ignoring instructions on legal strategy.

Paschke's report, which followed a two-month investigation of the court, was most harsh on abuses in the registrar's department. Adede himself was cited for spending nearly half his time on official travel.

But Paschke said he did not recommend Adede be dismissed because of the many complex tasks he managed to carry out in setting up a new centre with hardly any support or proper backup from New York headquarters.
U.N. sources said Annan had not reached a decision yet on Adede's future.

The report also criticised the New York departments of legal affairs human resources and administration and management for abdicating their responsibilities and neglecting the tribunal, particularly in its start-up phase.
